commentary.bottom_line: Nine studies, all offline or simulated and most with small samples, suggest that expert feedback during development may improve the concordance, relevance, and safety review of specialized AI tools. No study measured patient outcomes in live care, so the recommendation rests mainly on professional consensus and one Utah statute.

perspectives.view: Seven level 4 and two level 5 studies all favor expert involvement, so the direction of findings is consistent. Every study was offline or simulated. Samples ranged from one development run to 516 social media posts, and none compared patient outcomes. Indirectness and imprecision lower certainty to very low.

A fully automated algorithm build produced 17 issues, 9 high priority, while an expert-governed build needed no mandatory safety corrections. Human judgment remained necessary to detect subtle reasoning failures, and expert oversight identified data bias and leakage. A trial in which a data-tuned model omitted diagnoses in 30.0% of cases shows the hazard but did not test expert review.

Pathologist-in-loop fine-tuning raised agreement from 81.8% to 96.4% (κ 0.62 to 0.91), and tumor board feedback raised semantic similarity from 0.71 to 0.76. Expert-authored prompt framing reached 0.562 macro F1 versus 0.395 for moderation APIs. These gains were measured offline, and fidelity in routine development workflows remains unknown.

Expert time is the main cost. The fully automated algorithm build ran 3.6 times faster than the expert-governed build, and automated screening reduced but did not replace expert review burden. No study reported staff hours, cost, or the number of experts needed per tool, so budgeting will depend on local estimates.

Two tests took place in non-English settings, a Korean chatbot pilot with 15 graduate students and an Italian extraction study. No test enrolled Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy users. The trial documenting the hazard included rural, low-income, and low-literacy patients in China, which suggests these groups face the problem the practice targets.

In the only test with end users, 13 of 15 participants preferred a mental health chatbot after expert-guided enhancement, and ratings rose from 5.40 to 7.63. Participants were graduate students rather than patients, so the result says little about whether people in distress would trust such tools or could reach a human when needed.

Utah HB 452 requires mental health chatbots to be developed and monitored consistent with clinical best practices, and NIST AI 600-1 recommends human moderation of generated content. Neither source defines who qualifies as an expert or what a review must document. None of the supplied studies tests compliance with these provisions.

commentary.research_gap: No study compared expert involvement with its absence in a live clinical deployment that measured patient outcomes. Prospective comparisons, ideally randomized, of expert-reviewed and unreviewed specialized tools, including mental health chatbots, would address this gap if they reported safety events, clinical accuracy, expert hours, and results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, and low-literacy users.
commentary.underserved_note: Two tests included non-English-speaking populations in South Korea and Italy, but neither enrolled patients, and no test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations. The hazard trial in China enrolled low-income, rural, and low-literacy patients, so the problem is documented in these groups while the safeguard remains untested there.
